title: Rice Blast: How to Spot It and Stop It in Your Palay
metaTitle: Rice Blast: Signs, Damage and Control in the Philippines
metaDescription: Rice blast, or mata mata, can kill young palay and empty whole panicles. Learn to read leaf, node and neck blast and stop it before heading.
excerpt: Rice blast is the fungal disease many farmers call mata mata. IRRI ranks it among the most destructive diseases of palay (rice still in the husk). It spots the leaves, blackens the nodes and rots the neck of the panicle. A bad attack can leave few or no grains.

heroImage.alt: A rice leaf with a gray centered, spindle shaped blast lesion with a brown border
heroImage.credit: Unknown author, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

blocks.text:
Rice blast comes from the fungus Pyricularia oryzae, also called Magnaporthe oryzae. It can attack every part of the plant above the ground. That runs from the leaf and collar to the node, the neck and the panicle. PhilRice says it strikes where irrigation runs short and in upland fields. It does so most of all when the sky stays cloudy and rain keeps falling.

PhilRice handouts call it mata mata, the word for its spots on the leaf. A PhilRice disease poster also lists agupaw in Waray and taya taya in Cebuano areas of Mindanao. Blast hits twice. Early on it can kill seedlings and young plants. Later, neck blast cuts the panicle off right when the grain should fill. So the first defense is the seed you buy, and our guide to [rice varieties in the Philippines](/crops/rice-varieties-philippines) can help you choose.

blocks.caption: Quick facts
rows: Mata mata (Tagalog and Bisaya), agupaw (Waray), taya taya (Cebuano in Mindanao)
Leaves, stems and tillers, panicles and ears and seedlings
Blast can strike at any stage, but leaf blast hurts most from the seedbed to tillering, while node and neck blast hit as the panicles come out and fill, mostly in cloudy, rainy weeks.
The fungus survives on infected straw and stubble, and its spores travel through the air. When a spore lands on a wet leaf, it sprouts, enters the leaf and makes a spot that soon releases new spores.

blocks.text: Start with the leaves. Young spots are white to gray green with dark green borders. Older spots turn spindle or diamond shaped, wide in the middle and pointed at both ends. They have a gray center and a reddish brown border. Next, check the collar where the flag leaf meets the sheath, then the nodes and the neck below the panicle. A blackened node or a grayish brown rot at the neck means the fungus has moved up the plant.

items: Spindle or diamond shaped leaf spots with gray centers and reddish brown borders.
Whole leaves that dry out after many spots grow together.
A lesion at the base of the flag leaf, the collar, that makes the flag leaf dry up.
Nodes that rot and turn black, so the stem breaks and everything above it dies.
A grayish brown rot at the base of the panicle, so the neck snaps or the panicle turns white.
Discolored grains, or few to no filled grains when the neck was hit before the milky stage.

blocks.title: Do not confuse it with
blocks.text: Brown spot is the usual mix up. Blast spots are long and pointed at both ends, while brown spot lesions are rounder, brown and ringed with yellow. White panicles from neck blast also look like stem borer whiteheads. But a stem hit by a borer pulls out easily and a blast hit stem does not.
How Rice Blast Hurts Your Palay

IRRI calls blast one of the most destructive diseases of rice. Leaf blast can kill seedlings or plants up to tillering. On older plants, a severe attack shrinks the green leaf area that fills the grain. Neck and node blast hurt even more, because they hit the panicle directly. If the neck is infected before the milky stage, no grain forms at all.

There is no simple count that tells you when to spray. Instead, IRRI advises a fungicide at heading only where the risk of yield loss is high. PhilRice also warns that the disease keeps building as long as blast spores stay in the air. So a field that had neck blast last season needs a plan before booting, and nitrogen is a big part of it. Our guide to [fertilizer for rice](/blog/fertilizer-for-rice) shows how to split it.

items: Plant a resistant variety first. PhilRice lists PSB Rc10, NSIC Rc122, Rc242 and Rc300 among varieties that hold up against blast, and your local agriculture office knows which suit your area.
Sow clean, healthy seed early, soon after the rains begin. PhilRice prefers transplanting to broadcasting, and seedlings raised in a wet bed.
Split your nitrogen into two or more applications and never pile it on. PhilRice adds that nitrate nitrogen raises the risk more than ammonium nitrogen.
Keep water on the field. IRRI advises flooding as often as you can, and PhilRice says irrigation cuts the attack, most of all in rainfed areas.
Avoid close planting, and stay out of the field while the leaves are wet, since walking through a wet crop spreads the disease.
On soils short of silicon, IRRI suggests calcium silicate, or straw from high silicon rice that is free of blast.

blocks.text: A fungicide makes sense only when a susceptible variety meets wet, cloudy weather near heading. It also makes sense when the field had neck blast before. For neck blast, PhilRice advises two sprays: one as the panicles start to come out and another when about half have emerged. Follow the FPA registered label for the rate.

blocks.title: Spray safely
blocks.text: Use only products registered with the [Fertilizer and Pesticide Authority](/blog/fertilizer-and-pesticide-authority), and follow the label for the rate, the timing and the protective clothing. Switch to a different fungicide group next time, so the disease does not learn to survive it. Our [guide to plant diseases](/diseases/plant-diseases-philippines) explains how.

items: Choose a blast resistant variety, and ask your local agriculture office for the current list.
Use clean, healthy seed, as PhilRice advises.
Destroy or plow under infected straw and stubble after harvest, since spores survive there.
Rotate the field with mungo, pakwan, talong or mais when you can, as PhilRice suggests.
Feed the crop in split doses and keep the field flooded, instead of letting the soil dry out.

blocks.text: Questions Farmers Ask About Rice Blast

items.q: What is mata mata in rice?
items.a: Mata mata is a local name for rice blast, the fungal disease caused by Pyricularia oryzae. PhilRice uses it in its Tagalog handouts and lists it as the Bisaya name too. In Waray the same disease is agupaw.

items.q: How do I tell neck blast from stem borer damage?
items.a: Both leave white panicles, so tug the stem. A stem hit by the [rice stem borer](/pests/rice-stem-borer) breaks away where the larva bored in, but a blast hit stem stays attached.

items.q: When should I spray a fungicide for rice blast?
items.a: Only when the risk is high: a susceptible variety, a history of blast and wet, cloudy weather. IRRI says a spray at heading can work, and PhilRice suggests two sprays for neck blast.

items.q: Are my round brown spots blast too?
items.a: Probably not. Blast spots are pointed at both ends with gray centers. Round brown spots with a yellow halo point to [brown spot](/diseases/rice-brown-spot), which is common in poor, unflooded soil.
